messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 20
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Soldier
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 33

She is 20 years old, a young South Eastern Asian woman who still looks, at first glance, more like a student than a soldier. She is married, and when she talks about her husband, her face briefly softens, though even that softness seems guarded now. She enlisted early, drawn by structure, purpose, and the pride of doing something larger than herself. In the beginning, military life suits her. She likes the predictability of drills, the clear expectations, the physical challenge. She takes comfort in knowing what is required of her and in meeting those standards.

The assault happens after an evening gathering on base. She does not tell the story dramatically. In fact, the way she tells it is strikingly flat, as if emotion has been packed away so tightly that it can only leak out in small, unexpected moments. She remembers the fluorescent light in the hallway, the smell of sweat and alcohol, and the split second in which she realizes that the person in front of her is not going to stop when she tells him to. What returns to her most often is not the pain but the disbelief: the stunned thought that this is happening here, in uniform, in a place that is supposed to be safe. She remembers freezing. Later, this becomes one of the things she cannot forgive in herself, even though she knows, at least intellectually, that she had not chosen it.

In the days after, she continues to report for duty. She shines her boots, keeps her posture straight, answers questions with “yes, ma’am” and “yes, sir.” From the outside, she appears composed. Inside, her body feels unfamiliar. She startles at footsteps behind her. She avoids certain corridors and invents reasons not to be alone in particular buildings. At night she lies beside her husband awake for hours, every muscle tense, listening for sounds that do not belong in their apartment. When she does sleep, she wakes abruptly, heart pounding, caught in fragments of the assault. In the dreams she cannot move or shout. Sometimes she wakes already fighting, throwing an elbow or scrambling backward before she knows where she is. Her husband learns not to touch her unexpectedly.

She tells herself to push through. In the military, she is used to overriding discomfort. But this is different. During training exercises, if someone comes too close from behind, her chest locks and her mind seems to go blank for a second. She becomes hyperaware of exits, corners, and the distance between herself and other people. She studies every room she enters. In formation, she focuses so hard on staying in control that by the end of the day she is exhausted. She begins to dread ordinary interactions with male soldiers, not because each of them has done something wrong, but because her body no longer makes those distinctions quickly enough. She hates this change in herself. She had once felt competent and physically capable; now she feels as if her nervous system has become its own chain of command, issuing orders she never agreed to follow.

At home, her world shrinks. She used to call family often, but now she keeps conversations brief, not wanting to explain why she sounds distant. Her husband asks what she needs, and she says “I’m fine” so many times that the phrase starts to sound mechanical even to her. She feels guilty for being far away from the woman she was when they married. Intimacy becomes complicated. Sometimes she wants closeness and then, in the middle of it, panic rises so suddenly that she has to pull away and sit in the bathroom, shaking and ashamed. She worries he will see her as broken, though he has given her little reason to think that.

There are moments when the memory intrudes without warning. The sound of laughter outside a barracks room, the scent of cologne, a certain kind of heavy step in a hallway—these are enough to drag her back into the worst minutes of her life. In those moments, the present disappears. She feels her throat close, her skin prickle, her thoughts narrow to one urgent need: get out. She has left meetings abruptly, claiming nausea. She takes longer routes to avoid places associated with that night, even if it makes her late. She notices that she no longer relaxes anywhere, not fully. Even on her days off, she sits with her back to the wall in restaurants and scans the room before she can taste her food.

She is frustrated by how invisible all of this is. People see a disciplined young soldier, recently married, still performing her duties. They do not see how much effort it takes to step into uniform each morning, or how often she has to argue with herself just to enter buildings that remind her of what happened. She wants her old certainty back—her trust in her body, in other people, in the idea that she can tell danger from safety. Instead, she moves through the present as if the assault is not over but waiting, just out of sight, for one unguarded moment.
